name: Afamelanotide

lead: Afamelanotide (melanotan I, sold as Scenesse) is a prescription implant that increases melanin in the skin, so people notice a darker, more even tone. Tanning communities discuss it as the approved counterpart to melanotan II.

It activates the MC1R receptor on pigment cells, shifting production toward eumelanin, the brown-black pigment. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials were run in erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), where it increased pain-free time in light. Smaller studies have looked at vitiligo, acne and other conditions. No large trial has tested it as a cosmetic tan in healthy people.

paras: In its approved use it is a small implant placed under the skin by a specialist centre, with the darkening arriving as part of the treatment. Patients are monitored with regular skin checks. Cosmetic use sits outside what it is approved for.

In trials, adverse events were generally mild, most often headache, nausea and implant-site reactions. Skin darkening and changes in existing moles are expected effects, so regular skin checks are advised. It is prescription-only, costly, and available through specialist centres. Its safety data come from regulated clinical use and do not cover unregulated melanotan products.

angle.text: Afamelanotide darkens skin by activating the MC1R pathway, which raises melanin and gives a deeper, more even tone. That darkening is a side effect of its approved use for a rare light-sensitivity disorder, and tanning communities discuss it as a relative of melanotan II. Cosmetic use in healthy people has not been tested in large trials.

lead: Afamelanotide, sold as Scenesse and originally called melanotan I (also NDP-MSH or CUV1647), is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) delivered as a small subcutaneous implant. It is approved to reduce phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited condition in which light exposure causes severe pain [1][2].

For appearance, its relevance is the tan. It activates the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) on pigment cells, raising melanin production and darkening the skin without UV exposure as the trigger [1][2]. That is why it began life at the University of Arizona in the 1980s as a candidate sunless-tanning agent, and why looksmaxxing forums discuss it as 'melanotan 1', usually next to the unlicensed peptide melanotan II, which has a different structure and no approval [3][4]. Forum posters mention a deeper, more even tan, darker freckles and a tanned look year-round as the attraction [5][4][6].

The best-characterised evidence comes from two randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in EPP, in which implant recipients spent more pain-free time in sunlight [7][8]. Smaller studies have examined it in vitiligo (where pigment gain is the goal), acne, solar urticaria, Hailey-Hailey disease and other conditions [9][10][11][12]. The licensed product is a prescription implant placed by trained clinicians; products sold online as melanotan are a separate, unregulated market, and regulators in several countries have issued warnings about them [1][2].

paras: In the European Union, afamelanotide is indicated for preventing phototoxicity in adults with EPP; in the United States the label is to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with a history of phototoxic reactions from EPP [1][2]. EPP is a photodermatosis in which accumulated protoporphyrin causes painful reactions to light, and treatments had been limited [13].

Afamelanotide's tanning effect is why it appears in appearance communities. Posters on looksmax.org describe melanotan 1 as a gentler alternative to melanotan 2 for building a tan, and note it can darken freckles, which some regard as a desirable look [5][4][6]. Wikipedia and other references note that the original University of Arizona programme aimed at a sunless tanning agent, and that the product was initially described as a tanning aid [1][3].

The approved product is a prescription implant used through specialist centres, and the manufacturer is reported to restrict supply to medical use [3][2]. Products circulating in gyms, salons and online under the name melanotan are not the licensed implant, vary in quality, and are illegal for human use in many jurisdictions [1].

Erythropoietic protoporphyria: two multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, reported together in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2015, tested 16 mg afamelanotide implants every 60 days against placebo in 74 European and 94 US patients [7][8]. The primary endpoint was hours of direct sunlight exposure without pain. In the European trial (five implants over nine months) the median was 6.0 hours with afamelanotide versus 0.8 with placebo; in the US trial (three implants over six months) it was 69.4 versus 40.8 hours [8]. Adverse events were mostly mild to moderate; the drug-specific effect was implant-site hyperpigmentation, seen in about a third of recipients, and a few patients had darkened moles [8].

Earlier work included a 2009 report of clinical responses in EPP patients [13][14], a long-term observational study of 115 patients [15], and an immunogenicity evaluation measuring antibodies across phase 2 and 3 trials [16]. The label's safety data come from three vehicle-controlled trials involving 244 adults [2]; Wikipedia describes these as the basis of the 2019 FDA approval [1].

Vitiligo: a randomized multicenter trial compared an afamelanotide implant plus narrowband UVB (n=28) with UVB alone (n=27) in adults with non-segmental vitiligo [9]. An earlier report described four patients [17], and a randomized study examined the combination in Asian patients [18]. Reviews list afamelanotide among emerging vitiligo options [19].

Other conditions: phase 2 studies examined it in acne vulgaris [10][20], Hailey-Hailey disease [12] and solar urticaria [11]. Small registered studies cover xeroderma pigmentosum, DNA repair after UV in healthy volunteers, and acute ischaemic stroke [21][22][23]. An exploratory 2026 study assessed its effect on UV erythema and melanogenic responses in healthy humans [24]. These studies are small or exploratory, and none has led to a cosmetic indication.

In the US label's trials, through month six, implant-site reactions occurred in 21 percent of afamelanotide recipients versus 10 percent on vehicle, nausea in 19 versus 14 percent, fatigue in 6 versus 3 percent, skin hyperpigmentation in 4 versus 0 percent and melanocytic naevus in 4 versus 2 percent [2]. Wikipedia also lists headache (about 20 percent), back pain, dizziness, flushing, new moles and freckles [1].

The label warns of serious hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, in which case the implant is removed and no further doses are given, and of generalized skin darkening and darkening of existing naevi and freckles; it recommends a full-body skin examination twice a year [2]. No human data exist for pregnancy; rat studies at up to 12 times the human dose showed no adverse embryofetal effects [2]. Wikipedia describes the melanoma risk as unclear and notes that pigmentation changes can obscure monitoring [1].

Reports on unlicensed melanotan products (mostly melanotan II) include flushing, nausea, mole changes and, in men, erections; agencies in several countries, including the UK and Ireland, and the FDA (a warning letter in January 2009), began warning about them from 2007. A 2011 case report described melanoma in a melanotan user, while a 2021 review summarised on Wikipedia suggested higher melanoma rates among users may reflect heavy UV and sunbed exposure.

Afamelanotide is a synthetic tridecapeptide analogue of alpha-MSH that binds predominantly to MC1R. It resists breakdown by proteolytic enzymes and binds longer than natural alpha-MSH, producing darkening of the skin through increased eumelanin [1][3]. In EPP, the increase in pigmentation is associated with greater tolerance of light [7].

The molecule is a 13-residue peptide with a norleucine and a D-phenylalanine substitution relative to alpha-MSH, molecular formula C78H111N21O19, which makes it resist enzymatic breakdown and bind MC1R longer [1]. Its plasma half-life is only about 30 minutes, so a bioresorbable implant (a rod about 1.7 cm long and 1.45 mm wide, placed under the skin above the hip) provides sustained release: most is released in about two days and it is undetectable in plasma by day ten [1][2]. In EPP the implant is repeated about every two months [2][7].

Alpha-MSH was isolated in the 1950s and its role in pigmentation was understood by the 1960s [1]. Researchers at the University of Arizona created more potent, longer-acting analogues in the 1980s, including afamelanotide (melanotan I), followed by melanotan II, aiming at a sunless tan that might also protect against sun damage [1]. Grokipedia dates the licence to Epitan to 1999; Epitan became Clinuvel in 2006 [1][3].

Early formulations required many injections, so Clinuvel worked with Southern Research on a slow-release implant, ready by 2004 [1]. Trials from 2007 to 2011 covered several light-related conditions, then focused on EPP, and the compound received orphan-drug status in the US and EU by 2010 [1]. Italy's medicines agency approved it in May 2010, the European Medicines Agency followed around the turn of 2014-2015, and the US FDA approved it in October 2019 as a first-in-class drug [1][3]. The EMA reportedly widened the label in 2025 to allow year-round treatment [3]. Melanotan II meanwhile followed a separate path: Palatin Technologies dropped its sexual-dysfunction development in 2000 in favour of bremelanotide, and the compound moved into unregulated sale.

On looksmax.org, guides describe melanotan 1 and 2 together as alpha-MSH tanning peptides and some posts note that melanotan 1 can cause spontaneous arousal [25]. Forum users compare the two, describing melanotan 1 as having a more extensively researched safety profile and producing slower tanning than melanotan 2 [4][6]. Peptide products sold outside of prescription channels are not the licensed Scenesse implant.
Forum posters compare the slower, smoother tan of MT1 to the faster darkening of MT2 [4][6]. Wikipedia's Looksmaxxing article places off-label peptides in the 'hardmaxxing' category.

Scenesse is prescription-only in Australia, Canada, the UK, the US and the EU [1]. Melanotan II has no approval anywhere; Wikipedia describes the products sold online, in gyms and in beauty salons as not legal for human use in any jurisdiction, and says media have used the term 'tanorexia' for compulsive tanning culture around them. Forum guides, in contrast, describe peptide possession and import as legal in many places while sales are restricted [25].
Registered studies continue in xeroderma pigmentosum, facial vitiligo and DNA repair, mostly small phase 1-2 designs [19][21].
